title: Given the root of a binary tree, determine whether it is height-balanced, meaning that for every node the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by at most one.
shortTitle: Balanced Binary Tree — check height diff ≤ 1 at every node

s1_definition.profdef: A binary tree is height-balanced when, at every node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by no more than one. The efficient solution computes each subtree's height in a single post-order pass and simultaneously checks the balance condition, using a sentinel value such as negative one to signal imbalance and short-circuit the rest of the computation.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the bank's reporting tree and a rule that no manager's two sides should be lopsided, meaning one branch of reports cannot be much deeper than the other. To check it, each manager compares how deep their left team goes versus their right team. If any manager's two sides differ by more than one level, the whole structure is declared unbalanced, which matters because a lopsided tree makes lookups slow.
s1_definition.oneliner: At every node the left and right subtree heights must differ by at most one, checked in a single post-order pass that short-circuits on the first violation.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A binary tree is height-balanced when, at every node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by no more than one. The efficient solution computes each subtree's height in a single post-order pass and simultaneously checks the balance condition, using a sentinel value such as negative one to signal imbalance and short-circuit the rest of the computation.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the bank's reporting tree and a rule that no manager's two sides should be lopsided, meaning one branch of reports cannot be much deeper than the other. To check it, each manager compares how deep their left team goes versus their right team. If any manager's two sides differ by more than one level, the whole structure is declared unbalanced, which matters because a lopsided tree makes lookups slow.

**One line to remember:** At every node the left and right subtree heights must differ by at most one, checked in a single post-order pass that short-circuits on the first violation.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive approach computes the height of every node's subtrees with a separate recursion and checks the difference, which recomputes heights repeatedly and is order n times height, effectively quadratic on a skewed tree. The efficient approach fuses the height computation with the balance check so each node's height is computed once.

You write a helper that returns the height of a subtree, or a sentinel of negative one if any part of that subtree is unbalanced. The base case is a null node with height zero. For example: `if (node == null) return 0;`.

You recurse into the left child first, and if it returns the sentinel, you propagate the sentinel immediately without doing more work. For example: `int left = height(node.left); if (left == -1) return -1;`. You do the same for the right child. For example: `int right = height(node.right); if (right == -1) return -1;`.

You then check the balance condition at the current node: if the absolute difference of the two heights exceeds one, you return the sentinel. For example: `if (Math.abs(left - right) > 1) return -1;`. Otherwise you return the actual height, which is one plus the larger child height. For example: `return 1 + Math.max(left, right);`.

The top-level method declares the tree balanced if the helper does not return the sentinel. The time complexity is linear because each node is visited once and the balance check is constant work, and the space is proportional to the height. A senior nuance is the use of the sentinel to short-circuit: once a subtree is found unbalanced, there is no need to compute any further heights, and this early exit is what keeps the whole thing linear rather than quadratic.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, account records are indexed in a binary search tree, and lookups stay fast only while the tree is height-balanced. After a batch of inserts the operations team must confirm the index is still balanced, because a lopsided tree degrades lookups toward linear time. This is exactly how Balanced Binary Tree works — it verifies the height condition at every node.

Problem 2 — The check must be efficient over a large index and should stop as soon as imbalance is found. This is exactly why the solution fuses height and balance in one pass and short-circuits with a sentinel.

The mini-project builds an `IndexNode` class, a `BalanceCheckService` with the fused height-and-balance recursion and logging, and a runnable demo that checks a balanced tree and an unbalanced one.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the balanced tree rooted at 5000, with 3000 and 8000 as children and 1000 under 3000.

Step 1: The recursion descends to 1000, a leaf. Both children are null with height zero, the difference is zero which is within one, so 1000 returns height one.

Step 2: At 3000, the left child 1000 returned height one and the right is null with height zero. The difference is one, within the limit, so 3000 returns height one plus one equals two.

Step 3: At 8000, a leaf, both children null, returns height one.

Step 4: At the root 5000, the left child 3000 returned height two and the right child 8000 returned height one. The difference is one, within the limit, so 5000 returns height three. The helper never returned the sentinel, so the tree is balanced.

Step 5: For the unbalanced tree, the recursion descends the long left chain 5000, 3000, 1000, 500. At 500, a leaf, returns height one. At 1000, left height one and right zero, difference one, returns height two. At 3000, left height two and right zero, difference two, which exceeds one, so 3000 returns the sentinel negative one.

Step 6: Back at the root 5000, the left recursion returned the sentinel, so the root short-circuits and returns the sentinel immediately without even computing the right side. The tree is declared unbalanced.

```text
2026-10-26T20:00:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Account Index Balance Health
2026-10-26T20:00:00Z [INFO] Account index is BALANCED — lookups remain fast
2026-10-26T20:00:00Z [WARNING] Account index is UNBALANCED — consider rebalancing
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Balanced:        5000 (h3, |2-1|=1)
                  /     \
             3000(h2)  8000(h1)
              /
          1000(h1)
  → never returns -1 → BALANCED

  Unbalanced:   5000
                /
             3000 (left h2, right h0 → |2-0|=2 > 1) → return -1 
             /
          1000(h2)
           /
         500(h1)
  → root sees left=-1 → short-circuit → UNBALANCED
    (right subtree never even computed)
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Balanced Binary Tree ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Post-order DFS fusing height + balance check             │
  │  Sentinel (-1) short-circuits once imbalance found        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: Node holds key; Service checks balance                │
  │  O: tolerance (diff ≤ 1) isolated in one comparison       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   BalanceCheckService                 │
  │  + isBalanced(root): boolean          │ O(n) time, O(h) stack
  │  - height(node): int                  │ returns height or -1
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  Per node:
    left  = height(left);  if -1 → return -1   (short-circuit)
    right = height(right); if -1 → return -1
    if |left-right| > 1    → return -1
    else return 1 + max(left, right)

  Contract: true iff every node's subtree heights differ ≤ 1.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A binary tree is height-balanced when, at every node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by at most one. The naive way computes each node's subtree heights with a separate recursion and checks the difference, but that recomputes heights over and over and degrades to quadratic time on a skewed tree. My efficient solution fuses the height computation with the balance check in a single post-order pass, so each node's height is computed exactly once.

The helper returns a subtree's height, or a sentinel of negative one the moment any part of it is unbalanced. I recurse left first, and if it returns the sentinel I propagate it immediately without further work; I do the same for the right. Then I check the balance condition at the current node, returning the sentinel if the height difference exceeds one, and otherwise returning one plus the larger child height. The top-level answer is simply whether the helper avoided the sentinel.

The sentinel-based short-circuit is the whole reason this stays linear: once a subtree is known to be unbalanced, I stop computing heights entirely and unwind. The complexity is linear in time with space proportional to the height. Explaining why the fused pass beats the naive repeated-height approach is the point interviewers are checking.

In my project at National Bank of India, I used this on the account-number index, which is a binary search tree whose lookups stay fast only while it is balanced. After a batch of inserts, the health check confirms the index is still balanced, and if it is not, the service schedules a rebalance job, because a lopsided index drives lookups toward linear time. The short-circuit meant the check returned quickly even on a large index, stopping the instant it found the first imbalanced node.
